spans.note: title and Executive Summary heading

spans.assertion: after adjusting for position, league, games, height, and weight, there was no statistically significant difference in red-card rates between dark- and light-skinned players

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the adjusted risk difference was +0.21 percentage points (95% CI -0.02 to +0.44, p=0.079), not significant at α=0.05, with a CI spanning zero

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: there is substantial, statistically significant heterogeneity by league, and the overall null finding masks opposing league-level patterns
Germany shows a strong positive effect (+0.69 pp, p<0.001)
England shows a moderate positive effect (+0.38 pp, p=0.038)
France shows a negative effect (-0.46 pp, p=0.095)
Spain shows no effect (+0.01 pp, p=0.975)

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the skin tone × France interaction is statistically significant (p=0.001), indicating genuine effect modification rather than random variation

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported across all leagues combined, given the CI spanning zero, p>0.05, and heterogeneity

spans.note: separator and Section 1 heading (Primary Estimand)

spans.assertion: the primary estimand was defined as the adjusted percentage-point difference in P(red card) comparing dark-skinned (0.75-1.0) to light-skinned (0-0.25) players

spans.note: blank line and 'Result:' lead-in

spans.assertion: risk difference = +0.21 percentage points
95% confidence interval = [-0.02, +0.44] pp
p-value = 0.079 (two-sided, α=0.05)
standard error = 0.12 pp
z-statistic = 1.76

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.21 pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players, adjusting for covariates, but the difference is not significant and the CI includes zero

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the baseline red-card rate for light-skinned players is 1.21%, so the point estimate represents a 17% relative increase, with substantial uncertainty

spans.note: separator and Section 2 heading (Secondary Estimand)
'Result:' lead-in

spans.assertion: odds ratio = 1.19
95% confidence interval = [0.98, 1.44]
p-value = 0.079
log odds ratio = 0.173 (SE 0.099)

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: odds of a red card are 1.19x higher for dark-skinned players adjusting for covariates, and the CI including 1.0 is consistent with the risk-difference finding

spans.note: separator, Section 3 heading, and Unit of Analysis heading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad (N=99,645), each representing one unique pair with presence/absence of any red card across all their matches together

spans.note: blank line and Sample Composition heading

spans.assertion: total dyads = 99,645
unique players = 1,214
unique referees = 2,768
dark-skinned dyads = 15,990 (16.0%)
light-skinned dyads = 83,655 (84.0%)
total red cards = 1,241 (1.25% of dyads)

spans.note: blank line and Outcome Variable heading

spans.assertion: the outcome was operationalized as a binary indicator: any red card in the dyad (yes/no)
red cards are rare events, occurring in 1.25% of dyads overall

spans.note: blank line and Exposure Variable heading

spans.assertion: skin tone was dichotomized as Dark (0.75-1.0) versus Light (0-0.25)

spans.note: describes original data provenance: two independent raters coded skin tone from photos on a 5-point scale

spans.assertion: inter-rater reliability was r=0.92 with 76.8% exact agreement
the two raters' skin-tone scores were averaged into one score
the averaged skin-tone score was then dichotomized at the endpoints
dyads with middle skin tones (0.375-0.625) were excluded from the analysis

spans.note: blank line and Covariates Adjusted heading

spans.assertion: position (12 categories) was adjusted for as a covariate
position strongly predicts red-card risk (Center Backs 1.95% vs. Attacking Midfielders 0.68%) and differs by skin tone

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: league country (4 categories) was adjusted for as a covariate
leagues vary in racial composition (France 33.8% dark-skinned, Germany 8.8%) and referee culture

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: games played (continuous, 1-47 per dyad) was adjusted for as a covariate

spans.note: rationale: games as exposure time, no new decision or figure
blank line

spans.assertion: height (continuous, cm) was adjusted for as a covariate

spans.note: rationale: height as proxy for role/physicality
blank line

spans.assertion: weight (continuous, kg) was adjusted for as a covariate

spans.note: rationale: weight as proxy for playing style/physicality
blank line and Exclusions heading

spans.assertion: the original dataset had 146,028 dyads before exclusions
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin-tone ratings (players without photos)
17,015 dyads (11.7%) with middle skin tones were excluded to create clear comparison groups
7,471 dyads (5.1%) were excluded for missing position
686 dyads (0.5%) were excluded for missing height/weight
total excluded = 46,383 dyads (31.8%)
final analytic sample = 99,645 dyads (68.2%)

spans.note: blank line and Statistical Model heading

spans.assertion: logistic regression with a binary outcome (any red card) was used

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the model was specified as logit[P(red card)] with terms for dark skin, position, league, games, height, and weight

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the risk difference was estimated via marginal standardization: computing average partial effect from predicted P(red card|dark) and P(red card|light) per observation

spans.note: blank line and Standard Error Estimation heading

spans.assertion: standard errors were clustered at the player level to account for non-independence of dyads
clustering raised the SE from 0.080 (non-clustered) to 0.118 (clustered)

spans.note: blank line and Variable Transformations heading

spans.assertion: skin tone was averaged across raters then dichotomized (≤0.25=Light, ≥0.75=Dark)
red cards were dichotomized (any vs. none)
no other variables were transformed; all other variables were used as-is

spans.note: blank line and Missing Data Handling heading

spans.assertion: a complete-case analysis was used, excluding observations with any missing covariate
no imputation was performed for missing data

spans.note: separator and Section 4 (Conclusion) heading

spans.assertion: the overall conclusion is 'NOT SUPPORTED'

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the hypothesis is not supported by the analysis, though the point estimate is a small positive association (+0.21 pp)

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the finding is not statistically significant (p=0.079 > 0.05)
the 95% CI includes zero, indicating substantial uncertainty
the overall finding is contradicted by substantial heterogeneity, ranging from Germany (+0.69pp, p<0.001) to France (-0.46pp, p=0.095)

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the data do not provide sufficient evidence that dark-skinned players universally face higher red-card rates after adjusting for confounders

spans.note: blank line and 'However' transition into league-specific patterns

spans.assertion: in Germany there is strong evidence for the hypothesis (p<0.001)
in England there is moderate evidence for the hypothesis (p=0.038)
in France the pattern reverses (negative, not significant)
in Spain there is no evidence of an effect

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the heterogeneity suggests the relationship is context-specific, likely mediated by league-specific factors such as referee training, implicit bias, racial composition, and playing styles

spans.note: separator, Section 5 heading, and 5.1 Selection Bias heading
caveat about potential bias if photo availability correlates with skin tone and red-card propensity
blank line
caveat about whether excluding middle skin tones under- or appropriately estimates effects
blank line and 5.2 Measurement Issues heading
caveat that subjective skin-tone coding may bias estimates toward the null
blank line
caveat that dyad-level aggregation loses match-level context
blank line, 5.3 Confounding heading, and 'Unmeasured confounders' lead-in

spans.assertion: no direct measure of playing style or aggression (tackle frequency, foul severity) was available
yellow cards were used as a proxy for playing style/aggression in sensitivity checks
match-level factors (home/away, match importance, score differential) were not included
individual referee characteristics (tendencies, experience, training) were not included
player reputation (prior-card history, star status) was not included

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: specific tactical roles within broad position categories (e.g., defensive vs. attacking center midfielder) were not captured

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: implicit-bias (IAT) scores were available but not included as a covariate due to lack of within-league variation
the excluded implicit-bias measure may partially explain the observed league heterogeneity

spans.note: blank line, 5.4 Clustering and Dependencies heading, and 'Multiple levels of clustering' lead-in

spans.assertion: clustering of players within clubs was not adjusted for
clustering of referees within countries was not adjusted for
clustering of dyads within matches was not adjusted for (not observable in the data)

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: only player-level clustering was addressed in standard errors

spans.note: blank line and 5.5 Rare Events heading
lead-in noting red-card rarity leads to listed limitations
caveat: wide confidence intervals / low statistical power

spans.assertion: model convergence was successful despite rare-event concerns about instability

spans.note: caveat: difficulty detecting small effects
blank line and 5.6 Temporal Aggregation heading

spans.assertion: data were aggregated across players' entire professional careers

spans.note: blank line and 5.7 Generalizability heading
scope caveat: results specific to 4 European leagues, 2012-2013 season

spans.assertion: the analysis was restricted to male players and referees

spans.note: caveat: soccer-specific, may not generalize to other sports
caveat: single-season data, patterns may have changed
blank line, 5.8 Key Assumptions heading, and 'Logistic regression assumptions' lead-in

spans.assertion: the linearity-of-log-odds assumption for games/height/weight appears reasonable given their narrow ranges
there is no perfect multicollinearity; that assumption is satisfied
the independence-conditional-on-clustering assumption was addressed via clustered standard errors

spans.note: blank line and 'Marginal standardization assumptions' lead-in
caveat: model correct specification cannot be verified, residual confounding possible

spans.assertion: the no-unmeasured-effect-modifiers assumption is violated, as shown by the league heterogeneity

spans.note: blank line and 'Causal interpretation' lead-in

spans.assertion: given the observational design, the adjusted estimates were not given a causal interpretation and should be read as adjusted associations

spans.note: blank line and 5.9 Multiple Testing heading

spans.assertion: no correction for multiple testing was applied across the sensitivity and subgroup analyses
the primary estimand analysis was pre-specified/predetermined

spans.note: blank line, 5.10 Heterogeneity Robustness heading, and lead-in
possible explanation: true effect modification by league
possible explanation: confounding by unmeasured league-specific factors
possible explanation: sampling variability, despite significant interaction test
blank line
cannot definitively distinguish between the explanations

author's stated skeptical stance/motivation
blank line

spans.assertion: not statistically significant overall (p=0.079)
confidence interval includes zero (substantial uncertainty)
substantial heterogeneity, effect varies from +0.69 to -0.46 by league

spans.note: caveat: potential for unmeasured confounding (playing style, referee factors)

spans.assertion: the point estimate's effect size is small (0.21pp on a 1.25% baseline)

spans.note: blank line and 'However I cannot dismiss the hypothesis' lead-in

spans.assertion: league-specific effects in Germany (p<0.001) and England (p=0.038) are significant
excluding Center Backs yields p=0.045 (marginally significant)
the direction of the effect is consistently positive across most subgroups
the point estimate is positive in the main analysis despite not reaching significance

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: the data do not provide sufficient evidence that referees universally discriminate against dark-skinned players; the pattern is context-dependent
significant, substantively large league-level effect modification indicates institutional/cultural factors dominate any player-level skin-tone effects

spans.note: blank line

spans.assertion: any claim of bias should be league-specific (particularly Germany), not generalized to European soccer as a whole
the negative France effect suggests implicit bias may be weaker in more diverse contexts, explicitly noted as speculative
